title: Constitutional literacy is uneven: Americans recognize some high-salience rights and procedures while missing the wider system of government
source_unit: 2026 Annenberg Constitution Day Civics Survey by the Annenberg Public Policy Center; SSRS Opinion Panel Omnibus, August 6–9, 2026, 1,034 U.S. adults
geography: United States; nationally representative adults ages 18 and older

observations.period: 2024–2026; U.S. adults and knowledge of government branches

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the 2026 Annenberg Constitution Day Civics Survey

observations.method: Nationally representative SSRS survey fielded for APPC August 6–9, 2026; the report notes that 2024 and 2025 used different panels, limiting direct trend interpretation.
observations.uncertainty: The measure is an open-ended knowledge question with a ±3.5 percentage-point margin of sampling error; annual comparisons are affected by panel and field-method differences and do not establish the causes of knowledge change.
observations.counterinterpretation: Failure to name branches on demand does not prove inability to navigate government, vote, claim rights, or understand a specific political conflict; recall and civic competence are related but not identical.

observations.period: 2026; U.S. adults and First Amendment rights

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the 2026 Annenberg Constitution Day Civics Survey

freedom_of_speech.unit: percent naming freedom of speech in an open-ended question

freedom_of_press.unit: percent naming freedom of the press

right_to_petition.unit: percent naming the right to petition government

all_five_rights.unit: percent naming all five First Amendment protections

none_of_five_rights.unit: percent naming none of the five protections

observations.method: Open-ended APPC/SSRS survey question asking respondents to name specific rights guaranteed by the First Amendment.
observations.uncertainty: Open-ended recall depends on wording, prompting, education, media salience, and interview context; naming a right does not establish accurate legal understanding or use.
observations.counterinterpretation: The uneven pattern may reflect differential salience of speech, religion, press, assembly, and petition rather than a uniform absence of commitment to constitutional rights.

observations.period: 2026; U.S. adults and constitutional rights regardless of citizenship status

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the 2026 Annenberg Constitution Day Civics Survey

know_undocumented_people_have_constituti.unit: percent saying it is very or somewhat inaccurate that people in the U.S. illegally have no constitutional rights

say_no_rights_claim_is_accurate.unit: percent saying the claim is accurate

know_birthright_citizenship.unit: percent correctly saying U.S.-born children subject to its jurisdiction are citizens if neither parent is a citizen

observations.method: APPC/SSRS survey questions on constitutional protections and birthright citizenship.
observations.uncertainty: These are knowledge and belief measures, not legal-case analysis, immigration-status data, or evidence of how respondents would act in a policy dispute.
observations.counterinterpretation: Respondents may interpret the wording through current political conflict; agreement with the legal proposition does not reveal broader views about immigration policy, enforcement, or equal treatment.

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the 2026 Annenberg Constitution Day Civics Survey

know_veto_override.unit: percent correctly identifying the two-thirds override rule

know_5_4_supreme_court_decision_is_law.unit: percent correctly identifying that a 5-4 Supreme Court decision is law and must be followed

know_supreme_court_constitutionality_rol.unit: percent correctly identifying the Supreme Court's final responsibility when it disagrees with the president

know_tenth_amendment_states_rights.unit: percent correctly identifying the Tenth Amendment reservation of powers

unsure_tenth_amendment.unit: percent unsure of the Tenth Amendment relationship

observations.method: APPC/SSRS survey questions on veto power, Supreme Court authority, and federal-state powers.
observations.uncertainty: Correct-answer shares measure recall or recognition under survey conditions; they do not establish institutional trust, constitutional interpretation in live disputes, or effective civic participation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Knowledge may be issue-specific: respondents can understand a familiar veto rule while remaining uncertain about federalism or judicial review, so one score should not be treated as overall civic competence.

related_sources.claim: APPC archive and survey series context.

boundary: This record captures 2026 national estimates of constitutional and government knowledge among U.S. adults. It does not establish political competence, legal understanding, institutional trust, partisan meaning, civic education causes, voting, rights exercise, or democratic performance.
